newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK manufacturers set to shed stocks millstone.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK manufacturers set to shed stocks millstone.

text.p: Total stocks of unsold goods held by British companies fell sharply in the third quarter of the year, official figures showed, suggesting one of the major millstones for UK manufacturers is finally being eroded.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics on Friday showed total stock levels in the production, construction and distribution industries fell by 927 million pounds ($1.56 billion) in the third quarter.
"The stock overhang is coming to an end although it's not over yet," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Stocks in manufacturing fell by 176 million pounds over the past quarter having dropped by 215 million in the previous three months.

And Barr noted that the ratio of manufacturers' stocks to output had fallen again, to 90.6 percent in the third quarter from 91.6 in the second. Prior to the second quarter, that ratio had risen ever since late 1994.
"Manufacturers are much more optimisic now," Barr said.
Britain's manufacturing sector has been the poor cousin in an otherwise buoyant economy this year. Consumer spending has raced ahead but only now is the effect trickling down.
The key problems was that manufacturers put production into overdrive last year in response to healthy export demand.

But their European Union partners were struggling to squeeze their economies into the shape demanded by the Maastricht Treaty for a single currency -- pushing their economies close to recession. Demand for British exports dried up and stockpiles of unsold goods quickly snowballed. The ONS figures showed, for example, that in the third quarter of 1995, stocks increased by 1.255 billion pounds.
But while UK manufacturers remain blighted by weak demand from the European continent, with stocks evaporating they can at least gear up for the home market again.
The Confederation of British Industry's monthly trends survey, released overnight, also gave evidence of stock unwinding, albeit at a sluggish pace.

Of about 1,100 UK manufacturing firms surveyed by the CBI, 65 percent said stocks were adequate. Only five percent said they were less than adequate for current demand while 20 percent said stocks of unsold goods were still higher than they needed.
That gave a positive balance of 15 percent of firms saying stocks were too high. In October, the balance was 18 percent.

Sudhir Junankar, the CBI's associate director of economic analysis, said firms were starting to make a dent in their stocks of finished goods so the recovery in manufacturing output seemed likely to take root.
The survey also showed the balance of firms expecting to increase output over the next four months edged up to 21 percent in November, from 20 in October.

"It must be said that progress in reducing excess inventories remains slow," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident. "The outlook for manufacturing production is positive but modest as stocks remain high."
But Barr noted the CBI survey showed as many firms said order books were above normal as below -- the first time that balance has not been negative since August 1995.
The manufacturing sector cannot rest on its laurels just yet, not with the pound having rallied about 10 percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August, pushing up export prices as it goes.
"We would probably have a four percent plus growth forecast for manufacturing next year if it weren't for the pound," Barr said.

He said less than 50 percent of manufacturing output was exported and with the domestic economy so buoyant, producers can focus their efforts nearer to home. "But nonetheless, it will take the edge off any manufacturing recovery." ($1=.5937 Pound)
